summary: Updates the BGP Monitoring Protocol, which only exposed routes received from peers, to also give access to routes a router sends out. It adds a flag to the peer header to tell the received and outgoing tables apart. It updates RFC 7854.

plainLanguage.summary: BMP is a way for a router to show an outside observer the routes it has learned from its neighbours. This RFC adds the other half: showing the routes the router is sending out, so that an operator can check that it is advertising what it meant to.

questions: what is the bmp o flag
what is pre-policy vs post-policy adj-rib-out
subtitle: Lets BGP monitoring show the routes a router advertises, not only the ones it receives.

tldr.problem: The BGP Monitoring Protocol only exposed the routes a router received from its peers, so a service provider had no way to see what it was actually advertising, which matters when the customer at the other end cannot run monitoring itself.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a flag to the per-peer header so that a BMP sender can say whether a message carries the routes it received or the routes it advertises, and adds statistics for counting the advertised routes before and after policy.
tldr.outcome: The result is that outbound policy can be validated and audited the same way inbound policy already could be. RFC 8671 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 7854, and it was itself updated by RFC 9736.

today: RFC 8671 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 7854, and it was itself updated by RFC 9736. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: What BMP Could Not See
sections.content:
The BGP Monitoring Protocol (BMP) defines monitoring of the received Routing Information Bases (RIBs) per peer. The pre-policy Adj-RIB-In conveys to a BMP receiver all RIB data before any policy has been applied, and the post-policy Adj-RIB-In conveys all RIB data after policy filters or modifications have been applied. An example of the difference is when an inbound policy applies attribute modification or filters: pre-policy contains the information prior to those changes, and post-policy conveys the changed data or omits the filtered data.

Monitoring the received updates before any policy has been applied is the primary level of monitoring for most use cases. Enabling post-policy monitoring is mainly for inbound policy validation and auditing.

For a BMP receiver to receive any BGP data at all, the BMP sender, such as a router, needs an established BGP peering session and must be actively receiving updates for an Adj-RIB-In. Being able to monitor only the Adj-RIB-In restricts what data is available to BMP receivers. This is an issue when the receiving end of the BGP peer is not enabled for BMP, or when it is not accessible for administrative reasons. A service provider, for example, advertises prefixes to a customer, but cannot see what it advertises via BMP, and asking the customer to enable BMP and monitoring of the Adj-RIB-In is not feasible.

RFC 7854 only defines the Adj-RIB-In being sent to BMP receivers. This document updates the per-peer header defined in Section 4.2 of RFC 7854 by adding a new flag to distinguish between Adj-RIB-In and Adj-RIB-Out, and BMP senders use the new flag to send either one. Adding Adj-RIB-Out gives a BMP sender the ability to tell BMP receivers what it advertises to BGP peers, which can be used for outbound policy validation and to monitor routes that were advertised.
sections.plainLanguage: Monitoring could show you what a router learned, but not what it told the rest of the world. This RFC closes that gap.

sections.title: Pre-Policy and Post-Policy
sections.content:
Three definitions do the work. The Adj-RIB-Out is, as defined in RFC 4271, the table that contains the routes for advertisement to specific peers by means of the local speaker's UPDATE messages. The pre-policy Adj-RIB-Out is the result before applying the outbound policy to it, and would normally match what is in the local RIB. The post-policy Adj-RIB-Out is the result of applying the outbound policy, and it MUST convey to the BMP receiver what is actually transmitted to the peer.

Post-policy monitoring is the primary use case. It shows the updates transmitted to a peer after the outbound policy has been applied, so the result after modifications and filters. Some attributes are set when the BGP message is transmitted, such as the next hop, so only the post-policy view reflects them.

Pre-policy monitoring serves the same validation and auditing purpose as it does for the inbound side. A comparison between the two can be used to validate the outbound policy. What the candidate routes are depends on the type of the BGP peering session: internal BGP, an internal BGP route reflector client, external BGP, BGP confederations, or a route server client. The candidate routes that make up the pre-policy Adj-RIB-Out do not contain all the local RIB routes, so pre-policy Adj-RIB-Out conveys only the routes that are available based on the peering type, and post-policy represents the filtered and changed routes from the available routes.

Some attributes are set only during transmission of the BGP message, that is, post-policy. It is common for the next hop to be null, a loopback address, or similar during the pre-policy phase. All mandatory attributes, such as the next hop, MUST be either zero or have an empty length if they are unknown when the pre-policy phase completes, and the BMP receiver will treat zero or empty mandatory attributes as self-originated.
sections.plainLanguage: Two views of the same table. One shows the routes before the router's own filters touch them, and one shows exactly what went out on the wire. Comparing them is how you check that the filters did what you meant.

sections.title: The Per-Peer Header and the O Flag
sections.content:
The per-peer header has the same structure and flags as defined in Section 4.2 of RFC 7854, with the addition of the O flag. The header is eight bits wide and is laid out as the version flag V, the L flag, the A flag, the O flag, and four reserved bits. The O flag indicates Adj-RIB-In if set to 0 and Adj-RIB-Out if set to 1. The existing flags are defined in Section 4.2 of RFC 7854, and the remaining bits are reserved for future use; they MUST be transmitted as 0 and their values MUST be ignored on receipt.

When the O flag is set to 1, four fields of the per-peer header are redefined. The Peer Address becomes the remote IP address associated with the TCP session over which the encapsulated Protocol Data Unit is sent, rather than the local address used for the inbound case. The Peer AS becomes the Autonomous System number of the peer to which the encapsulated PDU is sent, and the Peer BGP ID becomes the BGP Identifier of that peer. The Timestamp becomes the time when the encapsulated routes were advertised, which can also be thought of as the time when they were installed in the Adj-RIB-Out; it is expressed in seconds and microseconds since midnight, January 1, 1970, UTC, a value of zero meaning the time is unavailable, and its precision is implementation dependent.
sections.plainLanguage: One bit in the header says whether the records that follow are about routes received or routes sent. When they are about routes sent, the address, the network number and the timestamp are read from the other side of the connection.

sections.title: Reporting Adj-RIB-Out
sections.content:
The primary use case in monitoring Adj-RIB-Out is to monitor the updates transmitted to a BGP peer after the outbound policy has been applied. These updates reflect the result after modifications and filters have been applied, for example post-policy Adj-RIB-Out. Because some attributes are set when the BGP message is transmitted, such as the next hop, the post-policy Adj-RIB-Out MUST convey to the BMP receiver what is actually transmitted to the peer. The L flag MUST be set to 1 to indicate post-policy.

Pre-policy Adj-RIB-Out is used in the same way as the pre-policy Adj-RIB-In: to validate and audit outbound policies. A comparison between pre-policy and post-policy can be used to validate the outbound policy. What the candidate routes are depends on the BGP peering session type, so pre-policy Adj-RIB-Out conveys only the routes that are available based on the peering type. The L flag MUST be set to 0 to indicate pre-policy.
sections.plainLanguage: The existing L flag already says whether a record was taken before or after the filters ran. This RFC just says the same rule now applies to the outgoing direction.

sections.title: BMP Messages and New Statistics
sections.content:
Many BMP messages carry a per-peer header, but some are not applicable to Adj-RIB-In or Adj-RIB-Out monitoring, such as Peer Up and Down Notifications. Unless otherwise defined, the O flag should be set to 0 in the per-peer header in BMP messages.

For Route Monitoring and Route Mirroring messages, the O flag MUST be set accordingly to indicate whether the message conveys Adj-RIB-In or Adj-RIB-Out. Statistics Report messages are not specific to either, so they MUST have the O flag set to zero, and the receiver SHOULD ignore it.

Four new statistics types are defined. Stat Type 14 is the number of routes in the pre-policy Adj-RIB-Out, a 64-bit gauge. Stat Type 15 is the number of routes in the post-policy Adj-RIB-Out, also a 64-bit gauge. Stat Type 16 is the number of routes in the per-AFI/SAFI pre-policy Adj-RIB-Out, structured as a 2-byte Address Family Identifier, a 1-byte Subsequent Address Family Identifier and a 64-bit gauge. Stat Type 17 is the same for the post-policy table.

A new Peer Up Information TLV type is also defined. Type 4 is the Admin Label, whose Information field contains a free-form UTF-8 string whose byte length is given by the Information Length field. The value is administratively assigned, and there is no requirement to terminate the string with null or any other character. Multiple Admin Labels can be included in the Peer Up Notification, and when they are, the BMP receiver MUST preserve their order. The Admin Label is optional.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC adds counters for how many routes are being advertised, and a way for the router to attach a label to a peering so that the monitoring system can tell groups of peers apart.

sections.title: Peer Groups and Admin Labels
sections.content:
Peer and update groups are used to group updates shared by many peers. This is a level of efficiency in implementations, not a true representation of what is conveyed to a peer in either pre-policy or post-policy.

One use case for monitoring post-policy Adj-RIB-Out is to validate and continually ensure that the egress updates match what is expected. Wholesale peers, for example, should never have routes with community X:Y sent to them. In that use case there may be hundreds of wholesale peers, but a single peer could have represented the group.

From a BMP perspective it should be simple to include a group name in the Peer Up, but it is more complex than that. BGP implementations have evolved to provide comprehensive and structured policy grouping, such as session, AFI/SAFI and template-based group policy inheritances, and that level of structure and inheritance does not provide a simple peer group name or identifier such as "wholesale peer". This document therefore defines the Admin Label type for Peer Up Information TLVs, which can be used instead of requiring a group name. These labels have administrative scope relevance: labels such as "type=wholesale" and "region=west" could be used to monitor expected policies. The configuration and assignment of labels to peers are implementation specific.

In case of any change that alters the behaviour of an existing BMP session, such as changes to filtering and table names, the session MUST be bounced with a Peer Down and Peer Up sequence.
sections.plainLanguage: There is no standard name for a group of peers, because routers group them in their own ways. So the monitoring system is given free-form labels to attach instead, such as "type=wholesale".

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The considerations in Section 11 of RFC 7854 apply to this document. Implementations of this protocol SHOULD require establishing sessions with authorized and trusted monitoring devices. It is also believed that this document does not add any additional security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing new is needed. The rules of the document this one updates still apply, and the monitoring session should only be with a device you trust.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
Three assignments are made in the "BGP Monitoring Protocol (BMP) Parameters" registry.

The "BMP Peer Flags" registry gains flag 3, the O flag, defined in Section 4 of this document. The "BMP Statistics Types" registry gains four values: 14 for the number of routes in the pre-policy Adj-RIB-Out, 15 for the number of routes in the post-policy Adj-RIB-Out, 16 for the number of routes in the per-AFI/SAFI pre-policy Adj-RIB-Out, and 17 for the number of routes in the per-AFI/SAFI post-policy Adj-RIB-Out.

The "BMP Initiation Message TLVs" registry gains type 4, the Admin Label, defined in Section 6.3.1 of this document.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA keeps the lists of BMP flags, statistics and information types, and this RFC adds one flag, four counters and one label type.
